passages.t: ‘Go back to the land of your fathers’
passages.happening:
Laban's sons are saying that Jacob has taken their father's wealth (verse 1). Jacob sees that Laban's face has changed toward him (verse 2).

“Then the LORD said to Jacob, ‘Go back to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you’” (verse 3).

Jacob calls Rachel and Leah out to the field (verse 4). He tells them that their father has “cheated me and changed my wages ten times, God has not allowed him to harm me” (verse 7). “Thus God has taken away your father’s livestock and given them to me” (verse 9). He tells them of a dream in which the angel of God said, “I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the pillar and made a solemn vow to Me. Now get up and leave this land at once” (verse 13).

The sisters answer together: “Are we not regarded by him as outsiders? Not only has he sold us, but he has certainly squandered what was paid for us” (verse 15). “So do whatever God has told you” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Twenty years after Bethel, God says, ‘Go back.’ He adds the same words as before: ‘I will be with you.’ At Bethel he promised, ‘I will bring you back to this land’ (28:15). Now the promise comes due.

Jacob meets his wives in the field, away from the tents, where no one can overhear. He is careful. He has reason to be.

His speech tells the story of chapter 30 from his side, and this time he gives God the credit. Laban changed his wages again and again. Whatever the terms, the flocks bore the young that went to Jacob. ‘God has taken away your father's livestock and given them to me.’ The peeled branches are not mentioned. The angel says, ‘I have seen all that Laban has done to you.’

God names himself ‘the God of Bethel’. He reminds Jacob of the pillar and the vow. The God who met a runaway on the road is the God who now calls him home.

Then, for once, Rachel and Leah speak with one voice. In that world a groom gave a payment for his bride. Jacob paid with fourteen years of work. The sisters say their father has kept it all and spent it, and treated them like strangers, as if he had sold them. They have no reason to stay.
passages.later:
God's words ‘I will be with you’ run from Isaac (Genesis 26:3) to Jacob (Genesis 28:15) to Moses (Exodus 3:12) and to the disciples: “surely I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

God saw what was done to Jacob, as he saw what was done to Israel in Egypt: “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt” (Exodus 3:7).
passages.asks: God said ‘Go back’ to a man who had been running for twenty years. Ask whether there is a place, a person or a question you have been avoiding that God may be calling you back to. Then remember that he says ‘I will be with you’ before he sends.

passages.happening:
Jacob puts his children and wives on camels and drives his flocks toward Canaan, to his father Isaac (verses 17-18).

“Now while Laban was out shearing his sheep, Rachel stole her father’s household idols” (verse 19). “Moreover, Jacob deceived Laban the Aramean by not telling him that he was running away” (verse 20).

He crosses the Euphrates and heads for the hill country of Gilead (verse 21). On the third day Laban hears. He chases Jacob for seven days and catches up with him in Gilead (verses 22-23).

“But that night God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream and warned him, ‘Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad’” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Sheep-shearing was a busy season that kept the owners out with the flocks. It gave Jacob his chance.

‘Household idols’ translates the Hebrew teraphim. These were figures of gods kept in the home. Some were small, small enough to hide in a camel's saddle, as here. One was big enough for Michal to lay in a bed in place of David (1 Samuel 19:13). They were used in seeking guidance by signs: Ezekiel shows a king consulting them (Ezekiel 21:21). Some scholars think they first stood for the family's ancestors. What they meant to Laban the text does not say, but he calls them ‘my gods’ (verse 30).

Why did Rachel take them? The text never says. Many scholars once explained it from clay tablets found at Nuzi, in northern Iraq, which were read to show that holding the family gods gave a claim to the father's estate. As the book page on Genesis explains, that reading has not held up, even for the Nuzi texts themselves, and scholars now use the Nuzi parallels with caution. Other suggestions are that she wanted the gods' protection on the road, or help to bear children, or that she meant to hurt a father who had sold her. These notes do not choose. The text leaves her reason unspoken.

‘Jacob deceived Laban’ is literally ‘Jacob stole Laban's heart’. The word ‘steal’ runs all through this chapter. Laban's sons say Jacob stole their father's wealth. Rachel steals the gods. Jacob steals away. Everyone accuses everyone else of theft.

Gilead is the high, wooded hill country east of the Jordan River. Laban rides hard for a week to catch them. And then God stops him with a dream. God protects Jacob, even though Jacob ran away in secret.
passages.later:
Once the family is home, Jacob tells them, “Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you” (Genesis 35:2), and buries them under the oak near Shechem (Genesis 35:4).

The prophets mock gods that must be carried: “They lift it to their shoulder and carry it along” (Isaiah 46:7), and “They cry out to it, but it does not answer” (Isaiah 46:7). Zechariah says, “idols speak deceit and diviners see illusions” (Zechariah 10:2).

Joshua reminds Israel that Abraham's family, Nahor included, “lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods” (Joshua 24:2).
passages.asks: Rachel left her father's house, but she took her father's gods with her. Ask what you carried with you from your old life that still has a hold on you. Then ask what it would mean to bury it, as Jacob's household later did.

passages.happening:
Laban catches up with Jacob in Gilead (verse 25). “What have you done? You have deceived me and carried off my daughters like captives of war!” (verse 26). He says he would have sent them off with music, and complains that he could not kiss his grandchildren goodbye (verses 27-28).

He admits, “I have power to do you great harm, but last night the God of your father said to me, ‘Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad’” (verse 29). Then: “why have you stolen my gods?” (verse 30).

“I was afraid,” Jacob answers (verse 31). “If you find your gods with anyone here, he shall not live!” (verse 32). “For Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols” (verse 32).

Laban searches Jacob's tent, Leah's tent, and the tents of the two servant women, and finds nothing (verse 33). Rachel has put the idols in her camel's saddlebag “and was sitting on them” (verse 34). She says, “Sir, do not be angry that I cannot stand up before you; for I am having my period.” Laban searches, but cannot find them (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Laban's speech is full of hurt feelings and a little false. He talks of music and goodbye kisses. Twenty years of changed wages say otherwise. Still, his complaint about his grandchildren may be real. He is a grandfather, and they left without a word.

Then he says something important. He could harm Jacob, but ‘the God of your father’ warned him. Laban is not a worshiper of the LORD, yet he obeys the dream.

‘Why have you stolen my gods?’ There is a joke the first hearers would enjoy. What kind of god can be stolen? These gods cannot protect themselves or tell their owner where they are.

Jacob's oath is rash and dangerous. ‘Whoever has them shall not live.’ He does not know that the one who has them is Rachel, the wife he loves. The reader knows. Some readers hear a shadow of this oath when Rachel dies on the road home (35:16-19). The text does not link the two, but the oath hangs in the air.

Rachel deceives her father, as Jacob once deceived his. She sits on the gods and says she is having her period. Israel's later law said that anything a woman sat on during her period became unclean (Leviticus 15:20). Laban's gods are hidden under a woman who says she is unclean. The story laughs at them.
passages.later:
A psalm mocks gods made by human hands: “They have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see” (Psalm 115:5).

Paul writes of people who “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

The God who stopped Laban in a dream is the one of whom the psalm says, “the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4).
passages.asks: Laban's gods could be stolen, hidden and sat on. Ask what you trust that cannot really protect you: money, a reputation, a plan. Then ask what it would mean to trust the God who protected Jacob when Jacob could not protect himself.

passages.happening:
Now Jacob is angry. “What is my crime?” he says. “For what sin of mine have you so hotly pursued me?” (verse 36).

“I have been with you for twenty years now. Your sheep and goats have not miscarried, nor have I eaten the rams of your flock” (verse 38). He says he never brought Laban an animal torn by wild beasts; he bore the loss himself. Laban made him pay for what was stolen by day or night (verse 39). “As it was, the heat consumed me by day and the frost by night, and sleep fled from my eyes” (verse 40).

Fourteen years for the two daughters, six for the flocks, “and you have changed my wages ten times!” (verse 41).

“If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with me, surely by now you would have sent me away empty-handed. But God has seen my affliction and the toil of my hands, and last night He rendered judgment” (verse 42).
passages.hearers:
Twenty years of anger come out at once. Jacob has kept quiet and worked. Now he speaks.

Shepherds in that world worked under agreements about who bore the loss when an animal died or was stolen. Israel's own law later said that a keeper who brought back the remains of an animal torn by a wild beast did not have to pay for it (Exodus 22:13). Jacob says he paid even for those. By any fair standard, Laban squeezed him hard.

‘The Fear of Isaac’ is an unusual name for God, found only in this chapter. Many take it to mean the God whom Isaac feared and worshiped, though scholars debate its exact sense.

Notice the turn at the end. Jacob does not boast of his cleverness. He says that if God had not been with him, he would have nothing. ‘God has seen my affliction.’ It is the same word Leah used when Reuben was born (29:32). The God who saw Leah has seen Jacob too.
passages.later:
Jesus contrasts himself with a hired hand: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep” (John 10:11). The hired hand runs when the wolf comes (John 10:12). Jacob was a hired shepherd who stayed through heat and frost. Jesus is the owner of the flock who gives his life for it.

Exodus uses the same words when God speaks to Moses: “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt” (Exodus 3:7).
passages.asks: Jacob worked faithfully for a man who cheated him, and God saw it. Ask whether you are working hard for someone who does not see or value it. Then remember that God sees your affliction and the work of your hands.

passages.t: Mizpah: a heap of stones between two wary men
passages.happening:
Laban answers, “These daughters are my daughters, these sons are my sons, and these flocks are my flocks! Everything you see is mine!” (verse 43). But he cannot do anything about it. “Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I” (verse 44).

Jacob sets up a stone as a pillar. His relatives gather stones into a heap, and they eat there by the heap (verses 45-46). Laban calls it Jegar-sahadutha, and Jacob calls it Galeed (verse 47).

It is also called Mizpah, “because Laban said, ‘May the LORD keep watch between you and me when we are absent from each other’” (verse 49). “If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives, although no one is with us, remember that God is a witness between you and me” (verse 50).

The heap and the pillar are witnesses “that I will not go past this mound to harm you, and you will not go past this mound and pillar to harm me” (verse 52). Laban calls on “the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor” to judge between them, and Jacob swears “by the Fear of his father Isaac” (verse 53).

Jacob offers a sacrifice and they share a meal (verse 54). Early the next morning Laban kisses his grandchildren and daughters, blesses them, and goes home (verse 55).
passages.hearers:
Laban still says, ‘Everything you see is mine.’ He cannot let go, even in words. But he knows he cannot win, so he asks for a treaty.

The two names mean the same thing, ‘heap of witness’. Jegar-sahadutha is Aramaic, Laban's language. Galeed is Hebrew, Jacob's. One family has become two peoples with two languages.

Mizpah means ‘watchtower’ or ‘lookout’. Laban's words, ‘May the LORD keep watch between you and me when we are absent from each other’, are sometimes used today as a warm blessing between friends who are parting. In the story they are not that. They are a warning between two men who do not trust each other. Laban means: when I cannot see what you are doing, God can, and he will judge you. The next verse makes it plain: ‘remember that God is a witness between you and me’.

The heap of stones is a border. Neither man will cross it to harm the other. Treaties in that world were often sealed with an oath, a sacrifice and a shared meal, and stones were set up as lasting witnesses. Gilead later became a border land that Israel and the Arameans of Damascus fought over for many years (1 Kings 22:3).

Laban protects his daughters in his own way: Jacob is not to mistreat them or take other wives. It is the first time Laban has shown much care for them. And he leaves with a kiss and a blessing. The parting is cold, but it is peace.

Notice the two oaths. Laban calls on ‘the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor’, Abraham's brother. He seems to think of more than one god. Jacob swears only by ‘the Fear of his father Isaac’.
passages.later:
Gilead was fought over for generations. The king of Israel asked, “Do you not know that Ramoth-gilead is ours, but we have failed to take it from the hand of the king of Aram?” (1 Kings 22:3). A town called Mizpah stood in Gilead in the days of the judges (Judges 11:29).

Paul gives a better pattern than a wary truce: “Do not repay anyone evil for evil” (Romans 12:17), and “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone” (Romans 12:18).
passages.hard:
The Mizpah words are often read as a sweet blessing for friends who must part. That is a fair use of the words for a prayer, if someone wants to pray it. But it is not what they meant here. In Genesis they are said by a man who has cheated his son-in-law for twenty years, to a son-in-law who has just run away from him in secret. They mean: ‘I do not trust you, so I am asking God to watch you.’

That is still a kind of peace. Two men who could not trust each other agreed not to harm each other, and called God as their witness. Sometimes that is the peace that is possible: a boundary, kept, with God watching. It is not the best peace, but it is better than war.
passages.asks: Jacob and Laban could not be friends, but they could agree not to harm each other. Ask whether there is a relationship in your life where a firm boundary is the most peace that is possible right now. Then ask God to watch over it, and to keep you from crossing it to do harm.
